summary: Days after US and Israeli strikes on Iran began on 2026-02-28, Iran declared the strait closed and traffic largely halted. Ships from states Iran calls non-hostile may pass through Iranian waters, reportedly for a toll, and in May Iran set up a Persian Gulf Strait Authority to run transits. The Commons Library cites WTO estimates of a 95% drop in crude carriers and 99% in LNG carriers from 28 February to 1 June. CRS reports a US blockade of Iranian ports from 13 April, a US-Iran memorandum on 17 June that briefly lifted crossings, and renewed attacks in July after which the US said the memorandum no longer applied. Start month is when PortWatch tanker transits fell, from 43.5 a day in February to 0.9 in March.

summary: On 2026-07-20 the Houthis (Ansarallah) declared a maritime embargo on Saudi Arabia, aimed at Saudi oil exports from Yanbu that had been running through the strait as Hormuz closed. CNBC reported a JMIC warning that the group had deployed missiles and drones near the strait, an EU naval mission advisory for ships linked to Israeli, US or Saudi interests to avoid the Red Sea, and Kpler data showing strait traffic down 34% the next day. On 2026-08-11 missiles struck the Egyptian-owned cargo ship Tihamah in the strait; Yemen's internationally recognised government blamed the Houthis and said at least six people were killed. PortWatch tanker transits averaged 11.6 a day in July and 8.5 in August.

summary: Underwater blasts ruptured both Nord Stream 1 pipes and one Nord Stream 2 pipe. Swedish and Danish seismic data showed two explosions; Denmark's prime minister said sabotage could not be ruled out. Reuters reported in March 2023 that the lines would be mothballed with no plan to repair them. On 14 October 2026 a former Ukrainian officer went on trial in Hamburg; German prosecutors accuse him of leading the operation for unidentified Ukrainian state entities. He and Ukraine's government deny involvement, and Russia denies blowing up the pipelines.

summary: QatarEnergy shut LNG production in early March 2026 after Iranian attacks and declared force majeure on its entire output. Missile strikes in mid-March damaged Trains 4 and 6 at this site, removing 12.8 million tonnes a year for three to five years, by QatarEnergy's estimate. With Hormuz restricted, Qatar's exports were about a third of pre-war levels in September, by Bloomberg's count, and under a quarter by Kpler's.
